  "title": "TokenSense: Task-Informed vs. Random Tokenization Diversity for LLM Reasoning",
  "core_problem": "Subword tokenization creates misaligned token boundaries for reasoning-critical content — numbers get fragmented inconsistently, dates split across semantic boundaries, and characters are absorbed into opaque multi-character tokens — causing measurable accuracy drops on arithmetic (up to +33.7pp recoverable from right-aligned digit grouping on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, per Broken Tokens), temporal reasoning (up to 10pp from date fragmentation), and character-level tasks (43.6% average accuracy on CharBench). Probabilistic Tokenization (NAACL 2025) proved that sampling 64 random alternative tokenizations with majority voting improves reasoning by +17.11% on average across seven base models and four benchmarks, confirming the problem is real and exploitable at inference time. Where is the Signal in Tokenization Space? (EMNLP 2024) provided theoretical grounding by proving that significant signal exists in non-canonical tokenization space. However, a fundamental empirical question remains open: does the SOURCE of tokenization diversity matter, or only its AMOUNT? Existing approaches are either brute-force (PT's 64x compute with no intelligence about WHICH tokenization helps for WHICH reasoning demand), narrow in scope (NumeroLogic handles only digit-count prefixes, ToCAD handles only character tasks, SepSeq handles only long numerical sequence processing), or operate across models rather than within a single model (SAFE/When to Ensemble uses tokenization mismatch between models as an ensembling signal). Critically, PT's impressive headline gains (+17.11% average relative) were measured on base models with low baselines (e.g., LLaMA-3-8B at 12.99% MATH, 37.71% GSM8k). On modern instruction-tuned models with verified baselines from the Qwen3 Technical Report Table 18 (Qwen3-8B non-thinking: 87.4% MATH-500; Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct: 77.6% MATH-500; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: 54.8% MATH-500), the absolute headroom varies substantially across models. Moreover, Broken Tokens showed that random non-canonical tokenization actually DEGRADES GSM8k by -6.1pp on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct (from their 87.3% canonical baseline under their evaluation protocol), suggesting that uninformed tokenization diversity may hurt more than help on strong models at small ensemble sizes. DivSampling (arXiv:2502.11027) demonstrated that task-specific prompt diversity outperforms task-agnostic prompt diversity for Best-of-N scaling with +10.8% reasoning and +9.6% math gains, but this principle has never been tested at the tokenization level. No controlled factorial experiment exists comparing task-informed vs. random tokenization diversity across model capability levels, aggregation methods, and ensemble sizes — and the question of whether instruction tuning provides implicit tokenization robustness that neutralizes the diversity-source advantage remains untested.",
  "opportunity": "Six converging findings create a clear empirical opening for a controlled investigation: (1) Broken Tokens (NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight) showed instruction-tuned LLMs retain ~93% performance under non-canonical tokenizations, but with ASYMMETRIC task-specific effects: character-level segmentation improves string tasks by up to 15%, right-aligned digit grouping improves arithmetic by +33.7pp, yet random tokenization DEGRADES GSM8k by -6.1pp on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct (from their canonical 87.3% baseline) — proving that tokenization perturbation is a double-edged sword whose effects depend on task alignment; (2) Probabilistic Tokenization (NAACL 2025 Findings) demonstrated that random tokenization diversity creates diverse reasoning paths, improving accuracy by +17.11% on average across seven base models — but whether task-informed diversity would outperform random at matched compute is unknown; (3) DivSampling (arXiv:2502.11027, Wang et al.) proved that task-specific prompt diversity outperforms task-agnostic prompt diversity for Best-of-N scaling with relative gains of 10.8% on reasoning and 9.6% on mathematics, establishing the principle that informed perturbation beats random perturbation at the prompt level — but this has never been tested at the tokenization level; (4) SAFE/When to Ensemble (Yun et al., ICLR 2026) showed that tokenization mismatch across models serves as a reliable signal for selective multi-model ensembling, ensembling <1% of tokens on MATH-500 while maintaining accuracy gains, and introduced probability sharpening for overly smooth ensemble distributions — establishing that tokenization alignment quality matters for generation quality, but operating inter-model rather than intra-model; (5) Dipper (EMNLP 2025) showed that principled semantic-volume-based selection of diverse prompt variants outperforms random selection at matched k, and that just 3 diverse variants of a 1.5B model can outperform a single 7B model; (6) CISC (ACL 2025 Findings) demonstrated that confidence-weighted majority voting reduces required self-consistency samples by 40%+ across nine models, proving not all reasoning paths deserve equal weight. The gap is a controlled factorial experiment varying diversity source x aggregation method x model capability x ensemble size, testing whether the informed-beats-random principle transfers from prompt-level to tokenization-level diversity, and whether instruction tuning neutralizes this advantage.",
  "landscape": "Where is the Signal in Tokenization Space? (EMNLP 2024, Geh et al.) proves that computing marginal probability over all tokenizations is intractable, yet demonstrates empirically that aggregating probabilities across non-canonical tokenizations improves LLM evaluation on multiple-choice benchmarks (HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, SocialIQA) for transformers (LLaMA 2, Gemma) and state space models (Mamba). This establishes the theoretical foundation that tokenization space contains exploitable signal, but operates in the scoring/evaluation setting. Broken Tokens (NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight, Zheng et al.) demonstrates that instruction-tuned models are robust to non-canonical tokenizations on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, OLMo-2-7B-Instruct, and Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, with task-specific gains from character-level (up to 15% string manipulation) and digit-grouped (+33.7pp arithmetic, specifically from 36.5% to 70.2% on a custom 10-digit benchmark with right-aligned digit grouping on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) tokenizations. Crucially, Broken Tokens reports that random non-canonical tokenization DEGRADES Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct on GSM8k by -6.1pp from their canonical baseline of 87.3% (note: Qwen's own evaluation reports 91.6% for the same model on GSM8k, a ~4pp discrepancy attributable to different evaluation protocols including prompting format, few-shot settings, and answer extraction methods; we cite Broken Tokens' 87.3% when calibrating against their findings and note the protocol discrepancy explicitly). Probabilistic Tokenization (NAACL 2025 Findings, Sathe, Aggarwal, and Sitaram) samples m=64 BPE tokenizations per input and uses majority voting, achieving +17.11% average relative improvement across 7 base models (OLMo-7B, Gemma-2B, Gemma-7B, LLaMA3-8B, LLaMA3-70B, Mistral-7B, Mamba-2.8B) and 4 benchmarks (MATH, GSM8k, AQuA, PIQA). Per-model results for LLaMA3-8B: MATH +17.45% (from 12.99% baseline), GSM8k +13.66% (from 37.71% baseline). Critical observation: all PT models are BASE models with low baselines — absolute gains are small (LLaMA3-8B MATH: 12.99% to ~15.3%, a +2.3pp absolute gain). When to Ensemble: Identifying Token-Level Points for Stable and Fast LLM Ensembling (ICLR 2026, Yun et al.) introduces SAFE, a framework that selectively ensembles multi-model outputs by jointly considering tokenization mismatch across models and consensus in next-token probability distributions. SAFE identifies that the standard practice of ensembling at every token often degrades long-form generation because tokenization divergence between models creates unreliable aggregation points. By ensembling fewer than 1% of tokens on MATH-500, SAFE outperforms existing ensemble methods in both accuracy and efficiency, with probability sharpening consolidating probabilities spread across sub-word tokens representing the same word. Key distinction from TokenSense: SAFE operates ACROSS models with different tokenizers, using tokenization mismatch as a NEGATIVE signal (avoid ensembling at divergent positions); TokenSense operates WITHIN a single model, using task structure as a POSITIVE signal (reformatting to improve tokenizer behavior). Both establish that tokenization alignment quality matters for generation quality, from complementary angles. SAFE's selective aggregation principle directly inspires our Q3 (does aggregation intelligence dominate diversity quality?). On the Effect of Sampling Diversity in Scaling LLM Inference (arXiv:2502.11027, Wang et al.) systematically studies diversity in scaling inference, demonstrating that responses from diverse prompts after Best-of-N selection exhibit significantly lower error rates than those from stationary prompts. They derive a diversity-fidelity tradeoff principle and propose DivSampling with task-agnostic and task-specific variants, where task-specific diversity yields +10.8% on reasoning (MMLU-Pro) and +9.6% on mathematics. This directly supports the hypothesis that informed perturbation outperforms random perturbation — but at the prompt level, not the tokenization level. NumeroLogic (EMNLP 2024, Schwartz, Choshen, Shtok, Doveh, Karlinsky, and Arbelle) applies digit-count prefix encoding to improve arithmetic in fine-tuned models. SepSeq (arXiv:2604.07737, Sun et al., April 2026) substitutes every k-th delimiter in long numerical sequences with a newline separator token, yielding 35.6% relative improvement across 9 LLMs via attention sink recalibration. SepSeq operates at the inter-number sequence level rather than the intra-number level, is mechanistically distinct (attention sinks vs. tokenization boundaries), and complements TokenSense's approach. The Sequential Edge (arXiv:2511.02309, Sharma and Chopra, November 2025) demonstrates that sequential refinement with inverse-entropy weighted voting outperforms parallel self-consistency in 95.6% of configurations at matched compute on large models (30B-235B), with gains up to 46.7pp. Inverse-entropy weighting assigns w_i = 1/max(H_i, epsilon). Dipper (EMNLP 2025) creates training-free inference-time ensembles via semantically diverse prompts, achieving gains with k=3-9 members on MATH, with semantic-volume-based selection outperforming random selection at matched k. CISC (ACL 2025 Findings, Taubenfeld et al.) introduces confidence-informed self-consistency, reducing required reasoning paths by 40%+ across nine models. VecCISC (arXiv:2605.08070, Petullo et al., May 2026) extends CISC with reasoning trace clustering, reducing token usage by 47%. Qwen3 Technical Report (May 2025) provides verified baselines from Table 18 (non-thinking mode): Qwen3-8B MATH-500=87.4%, AIME'24=29.1%, AIME'25=20.9%; Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct MATH-500=77.6%; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct MATH-500=54.8%. Table 6 (base models): Qwen3-8B-Base MATH=60.80%, GSM8k=89.84%. Table 17 (thinking mode): Qwen3-8B MATH-500=97.4%, demonstrating a 10pp thinking-vs-non-thinking gap. Word Recovery in Large Language Models Enables Character-Level Tokenization Robustness (arXiv 2026) reveals mechanistic in-group attention word recovery, raising the question of whether instruction-tuned models compensate for tokenization perturbations and whether this neutralizes diversity advantages — the basis for our Q4 (Diversity Collapse). No existing work provides a controlled factorial experiment comparing task-informed vs. random tokenization diversity across model capability levels, aggregation methods, and ensemble sizes for generation.",
  "inspired_by": "Pattern: DivSampling (arXiv:2502.11027) proved that task-specific prompt diversity outperforms task-agnostic prompt diversity for Best-of-N scaling with +10.8% reasoning gains. Dipper (EMNLP 2025) showed principled selection outperforms random in prompt ensembles at matched k. Broken Tokens (NeurIPS 2025) revealed the critical asymmetry: right-aligned digit grouping helps arithmetic by +33.7pp, but random tokenization HURTS GSM8k by -6.1pp on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct — meaning uninformed diversity is a double-edged sword. PT (NAACL 2025) showed random tokenization diversity helps base models (+17.11%), but whether this extends to instruction-tuned models or whether task-informed selection outperforms random at matched compute is untested. SAFE/When to Ensemble (ICLR 2026) showed tokenization alignment matters at the token level even for multi-model ensembles, and that selective aggregation can outperform comprehensive aggregation. Gap: No controlled experiment has tested whether the informed-beats-random principle (established at the prompt level by DivSampling and at the selection level by Dipper) transfers to the tokenization level, especially across the base-to-instruction-tuned spectrum where Broken Tokens showed effects reverse direction. Five genuinely uncertain questions emerge: (Q1) Do task-informed reformattings create cross-task interference? (Q2) Does the task-informed advantage grow or shrink with model capability? Competing predictions: variance-reduction theory (grows) vs. Word Recovery mechanisms (shrinks). (Q3) Does aggregation method dominate diversity source? SAFE's selective ensembling principle suggests aggregation intelligence may matter more than diversity quality. (Q4) Do instruction-tuned models exhibit diversity collapse under tokenization perturbation? (Q5) Is there task-dependent optimal ensemble size? Combination: task-aware input reformatting to steer standard tokenizers toward favorable boundaries + task-adaptive aggregation + controlled factorial design to answer genuinely open questions about the efficiency-of-diversity hypothesis at the tokenization level.",
  "approach": "We propose TokenSense, organized as a controlled factorial experiment to answer five genuinely uncertain empirical questions about tokenization diversity in LLM reasoning. The paper's primary contribution is the empirical answers to these open questions — along with comprehensive Pareto analysis and a large controlled dataset — not the system architecture. The experiment has four factors: (A) Diversity source: task-informed reformatting vs. random BPE sampling (PT-style) vs. canonical (no perturbation). (B) Aggregation method: uniform majority voting vs. CISC-style confidence-weighted voting vs. inverse-entropy weighting (Sequential Edge-style, w_i = 1/max(H_i, epsilon)) vs. oracle upper bound. (C) Model capability level: LLaMA-3-8B base (MATH ~13%, GSM8k ~38%, for direct PT comparison), Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (MATH-500 54.8% per Qwen3 Table 18, moderate headroom), Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct (MATH-500 77.6%, GSM8k 87.3% per Broken Tokens protocol, Broken Tokens degradation data available), Qwen3-8B non-thinking (MATH-500 87.4% per Qwen3 Table 18, near-ceiling stress test). (D) Ensemble size k in {1, 3, 5, 10, 20, 64}. Phase 1 — Definitive Baseline Establishment (Weeks 1-2): Run each model on each benchmark with canonical tokenization under our exact evaluation protocol. This resolves conflicting baselines: Broken Tokens reports 87.3% GSM8k for Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct while Qwen reports 91.6%, a ~4pp discrepancy attributable to evaluation protocol differences. All subsequent comparisons use our internally-consistent baselines. Phase 2 — Task-Aware Input Analysis and Reformatting Implementation: A lightweight, fully rule-based subtask detector identifies reasoning-critical segments using regex patterns and structural heuristics. For each detected subtask type, input text is reformatted for favorable token boundaries: (a) arithmetic: digits space-separated with optional place-value annotation or right-aligned comma grouping, following R2L alignment; (b) temporal: dates normalized to minimize fragmentation per mDFR metric; (c) character-level: characters space-separated with positional markers per ToCAD principle; (d) mixed/semantic: canonical preserved. Tokenizer verification confirms intended boundaries. For multi-type inputs with overlapping demands, separate ensemble members are generated for each strategy rather than merging conflicting reformattings; canonical input always serves as one member. Phase 3 — Full Factorial Sweep (Weeks 3-7): For each (model, benchmark, diversity source, aggregation, k) combination, generate k tokenization variants, collect full reasoning chains with logits, and aggregate. Record: (i) final accuracy, (ii) reasoning chain diversity metrics (edit distance, structural alignment, agreement rate before aggregation) for Q4, (iii) per-reformatting-strategy contributions for Q1, (iv) Pareto coordinates (accuracy vs. FLOPs). Phase 4 — Analysis Organized Around Five Open Questions (Weeks 8-10): Q1 (Interaction Effects): Does character-level reformatting help character tasks but hurt arithmetic on mixed inputs? We test with multi-type evaluation sets, comparing single-strategy vs. compositional reformatting. Prediction: interference exists, but magnitude uncertain. A SURPRISING finding would be that cross-task interference is severe enough to make task-informed reformatting WORSE than random BPE on mixed tasks. Q2 (Scale Sensitivity): Does the task-informed advantage grow or shrink across the 4-model capability spectrum (12.99% to 87.4% MATH-500 baselines)? COMPETING PREDICTIONS: variance-reduction theory (random BPE includes harmful tokenizations whose damage grows at higher baselines, per Broken Tokens -6.1pp) predicts advantage GROWS. Word Recovery mechanisms and instruction-tuning robustness (93.4% retention) predict advantage SHRINKS. A SURPRISING finding would be a non-monotonic relationship (advantage peaks at moderate capability). Q3 (Aggregation-Diversity Interaction): Does aggregation method matter more than diversity source? We directly compare CISC-weighted random tokenizations vs. uniformly-voted task-informed tokenizations at matched k. SAFE's principle that selective aggregation at <1% of tokens outperforms comprehensive aggregation motivates this question. A SURPRISING finding: if CISC-weighted random beats uniformly-voted task-informed, this shifts the research agenda from better diversity to better aggregation. We also test whether inverse-entropy weighting (Sequential Edge) outperforms CISC on math despite EDIS being designed for that domain. Q4 (Diversity Collapse): Do different tokenizations produce genuinely different reasoning chains on instruction-tuned models? We measure chain-level diversity (edit distance, answer agreement before aggregation) across models. A SURPRISING finding: if diversity collapse is near-complete on strong instruction-tuned models (chains near-identical despite different tokenizations), the entire tokenization diversity paradigm is undermined for production models, and the community should redirect to other diversity dimensions. Q5 (Optimal k per Task): Is there task-dependent k* below which adding variants hurts? If arithmetic saturates at k=2-3 while temporal benefits from k=5+, this implies fundamentally different diversity-accuracy tradeoffs across task types. Expected Effect Sizes (literature-grounded): For task-informed k=5 vs. canonical k=1 (absolute pp): LargeNumArith (custom 1000-problem 10-digit benchmark): +15-30pp base, +10-25pp instruct. CharBench: +5-12pp. MultiTempBench: +3-8pp. MATH-500: +3-7pp on LLaMA-3-8B (~13%), +2-5pp on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (~55%), +1-3pp on Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct (~78%), +0.5-2pp on Qwen3-8B (~87%). GSM8k: +3-8pp base, +1-3pp instruct. For the CRITICAL task-informed vs. random comparison at matched k=5, expected advantage is 30-50% of total tokenization benefit, but this is the most uncertain prediction and core question. Statistical Power: McNemar's test at alpha=0.05, power=0.80 with bootstrap CIs (10,000 resamples): LargeNumArith (n=1000) MDE ~3pp — well-powered. CharBench (n=1000+) MDE ~3pp — well-powered. GSM8k (n=1319) MDE ~2.5pp — borderline for instruct. MATH-500 (n=500) MDE ~4-5pp — sufficient for base. AIME24+AMC23 (~80) MDE ~12-15pp — qualitative only. Pilot study (100 examples per benchmark) before full evaluation. Plan B: If task-informed provides no advantage over random on instruction-tuned models, the paper becomes 'Instruction tuning neutralizes tokenization diversity source effects,' contradicting extension of DivSampling and Dipper to tokenization level. Publishable because: contradicts published results, has practical implications, raises theoretical questions about Word Recovery and instruction tuning. Pareto analysis, diversity collapse measurements, and ~50,000+ response dataset retain standalone value.",

  "description": "TokenSense is a controlled empirical investigation of whether task-informed tokenization diversity outperforms random tokenization diversity for LLM reasoning, organized around five genuinely uncertain research questions where EITHER answer advances understanding. The paper's primary contribution is the empirical answers to these open questions — along with a comprehensive Pareto frontier analysis and a large controlled dataset of model responses under systematic tokenization perturbations — not the system architecture.\n\nThe investigation is motivated by a convergence of findings that create genuine empirical uncertainty: DivSampling (arXiv:2502.11027) proved task-specific diversity beats task-agnostic at the prompt level (+10.8% reasoning gains), Dipper (EMNLP 2025) showed principled selection beats random for prompt ensembles, and Broken Tokens (NeurIPS 2025) showed random tokenization DEGRADES instruction-tuned models on GSM8k by -6.1pp (from their canonical 87.3% baseline for Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct under their evaluation protocol) while task-specific reformatting dramatically helps (+33.7pp arithmetic) — suggesting the informed-beats-random principle should transfer to tokenization diversity. However, SAFE/When to Ensemble (ICLR 2026) demonstrated that tokenization mismatch is primarily useful as a signal for AVOIDING aggregation at misaligned positions (ensembling <1% of tokens on MATH-500), and Word Recovery mechanisms (arXiv 2026) suggest instruction-tuned models may have learned to compensate for tokenization perturbations entirely. These competing pressures make the outcome genuinely uncertain.\n\nBaseline reconciliation is explicit throughout. Qwen3 Technical Report Table 18 provides verified non-thinking mode baselines: Qwen3-8B MATH-500 = 87.4%, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct MATH-500 = 54.8%, Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct MATH-500 = 77.6%. For GSM8k, Broken Tokens reports 87.3% for Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct under their protocol while Qwen's official evaluation reports 91.6%, a ~4pp gap attributable to evaluation methodology (prompting format, few-shot settings, answer extraction). When calibrating against Broken Tokens' -6.1pp degradation finding, we use their 87.3% baseline since the degradation was measured relative to that value.
